title: 10 Gifts for Someone Who Has Everything
summary: Ten gifts for someone who has everything, from information about their own health to experiences, services, and repairs, with what to check first.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


For someone who has everything, stop looking for a better object and change the category. Five things cannot be bought and stored, and they are where the good answers live: information they do not have, time and attention, experiences with a date attached, services that remove work, and consumables that get used up. The ten ideas below all come from those five categories, which is why they work for a person whose house is already full.


## 10 gifts for someone who has everything


The person who has everything usually has everything material. What they rarely have is unclaimed time, an honest picture of their own health, or someone who noticed exactly which recurring annoyance to take away. Pick from the table, then read the section for what to check before buying.


Gift idea Why it works for this recipient What to check before buying


Information about their own health It is the one thing money has not already bought them Their interest, consent, and current details on the gift page


A consumable at a quality they would not buy It gets used up and leaves nothing to store Their actual tastes, allergies, and storage


An experience with a date on the calendar It becomes a memory rather than an object The date, their schedule, and whether they want company


A service that removes a recurring chore It returns hours, which they are genuinely short of Which chore, access to their home, and how long it runs


A repair, restoration, or upgrade It improves something they already value The item’s condition, the specialist, and sentimental risk


A membership or access rather than a thing It opens a place, not a shelf Distance, opening hours, and whether they would go


Your time and a skill they do not have Nobody else can buy it for them What they actually need, and your honest availability


A contribution to something specific It reflects attention rather than budget A cause they named, not one you assume


Something archival and personal It cannot be replaced or repurchased Photo sources, accuracy of names, and their appetite for it


A gift that happens later, already booked It gives them something to look forward to Dates, deposits, and cancellation terms


## 1. Information they do not have about their own health


Information is the one category a full house cannot absorb, and health is the version of it that people who have everything most often lack.[Lipoprotein(a)](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/lipoprotein-a) is the clearest example: it is largely genetically determined, so it is usually measured once rather than tracked, and it is not part of the standard cholesterol result most people have already seen.[ApoB](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/apolipoprotein-b) sits next to it as a count of the cholesterol-carrying particles in circulation, which is a more specific number than the total cholesterol figure almost everyone has. Neither is something money has already bought them. A[Mito Health gift](https://mitohealth.com/gift) is one way to give that, and the gift page carries the current purchase, redemption, and eligibility details. Check that they want this kind of gift before buying, since health information is personal and their results are private to them. If they are the sort of person who enjoys tracking their own numbers, our[biological age testing guide](https://mitohealth.com/blog/biological-age-testing-guide-everything-you-need-to-know) explains what those measures can and cannot tell them.


## 2. A consumable at a quality they would never buy for themselves


A consumable suits this recipient because it disappears, which is exactly the point. Very good coffee, a single-estate olive oil, an unusual tea, proper chocolate, or a case of something they drink but always buy on offer all get used and leave nothing behind. Check their actual tastes rather than the impressive option, confirm allergies and anything they avoid, and check the storage requirements before sending something that needs a cold room they do not have.


## 3. An experience with a date already on the calendar


An experience works for someone who has everything because it converts into a memory rather than a possession. The important part is the date: an open-ended voucher becomes an obligation, while a booked evening becomes a plan. Check their schedule before booking rather than after, ask yourself honestly whether they want your company or their own, and choose a rescheduling policy that survives a busy month.


## 4. A service that removes a recurring chore


A service suits a recipient who is short of hours rather than money. A cleaner for three months, a gardener booked for a block of visits, a laundry service, a window cleaner, or a standing dog walk each return time on a repeating basis. Check which chore they would actually hand over, since people are particular about their homes, confirm they are comfortable with access arrangements, and be clear about how long the gift runs so it does not turn into an awkward invoice later.


## 5. A repair, restoration, or upgrade of something they already love


A repair suits the person who has everything because it improves a thing they already chose. A watch serviced, a leather bag restored, knives sharpened and rehandled, a bike rebuilt, a favorite jacket relined, or old family photographs digitized all qualify. Check the item’s condition with a specialist first, use someone with a real reputation rather than the cheapest quote, and ask before taking anything sentimental away, because a surprise restoration of the wrong item is hard to undo.


## 6. A membership or access rather than an object


A membership gives them somewhere to go rather than something to keep. A museum or gallery membership, a botanical garden, a climbing wall, a lido, a cinema club, or a library of specialist equipment all fit. Check the distance from their home, because anything over half an hour away is rarely used more than twice, confirm the opening hours suit their week, and be honest about whether this is somewhere they would choose to go or somewhere you would.


## 7. Your time and a skill they do not have


Your own time and skill is the only gift on this list that nobody else can buy for them. If you can cook, build, code, edit, drive, garden, or make things, offer a specific piece of it: a meal a month, a wall painted, a website fixed, a hedge dealt with. Check what they actually need rather than what you most like doing, put it in writing so it is a real gift, and only promise the amount of time you can genuinely deliver.


## 8. A contribution in their name to something specific they care about


A contribution works when it is precise. A donation to the exact organization they have mentioned, a tree planted somewhere they know, a subscription for someone else in their name, or support for a local project they follow all read as attention rather than as a way out of choosing. Check that you are naming a cause they have actually raised, avoid substituting a charitable gift for a present they were looking forward to, and keep it to a size that does not create an obligation.


## 9. Something archival and personal


Archival gifts cannot be repurchased, which makes them the exception to the rule that this recipient needs nothing. A printed photo book covering a specific year, a recorded interview with an older relative, a map of somewhere that matters to them, or a written letter naming real things all work. Check that you have the photographs before you promise the book, confirm the spelling of names and places, and judge their appetite honestly, because not everyone wants a sentimental gift opened in company.


## 10. A gift that happens later, already booked


A future gift gives them something to look forward to, which is its own value for someone whose immediate wants are already met. A trip booked for spring, a course that starts next term, a block of tickets for a series, or a seat at a supper club all extend the gift past the day they open it. Check the dates against their commitments, confirm what the deposit covers, and read the cancellation terms before booking anything far ahead. If you are choosing at the last moment, our guide to[last minute gifts](https://mitohealth.com/blog/last-minute-gifts) covers what can still be arranged today.


## What is the perfect gift for someone who has everything?


There is no perfect object for someone who has everything, because the problem is the category rather than the choice within it. The reliable answers are information they do not have, time and attention, an experience with a date attached, a service that removes work, and a consumable that gets used up. Pick the category that matches what they are actually short of, and the specific gift becomes much easier to choose.


## What can you buy a person who has everything?


You can buy them time, access, expertise, and information, all of which are purchasable and none of which take up space. A cleaner for three months, a museum membership, a coaching session, a watch service, preventive health testing, or a booked trip are all things you can pay for today. What you cannot usefully buy is another object in a category they already own well.


## What is the 5 gift rule for adults?


The five gift rule is a budgeting convention rather than a tradition, usually described as something they want, something they need, something to wear, something to read, and a fifth category such as something to do or something to share. Families use it to cap spending and to stop every gift being a variation on the same idea. For someone who already has everything, the “want” and “need” slots are the hard ones, and that is where a service, an experience, or information usually belongs.


## What is the 7 gift rule?


The seven gift rule is an expanded version of the same idea, and the exact categories vary between the families who use it. Most versions keep want, need, wear, and read, then add categories such as something to do, something to share, and something handmade. Treat it as a prompt for variety rather than a fixed list, and do not fill a category with something nobody wanted simply to reach seven.


## Can you give someone a health test as a gift?


Yes, you can give someone access to health testing when they want it and remain in control of whether and how to use it. It also holds up for the recipient who already owns everything, because a number about their own body is not something they could have picked up themselves without deciding to. A[Mito Health gift](https://mitohealth.com/gift) leaves that decision with them, and their results go to them and not to you. Talk it over first and check the current gift details rather than choosing testing on their behalf. For recipient-specific lists that use the same principle, see our guides to[health and wellness gifts for grandparents](https://mitohealth.com/blog/gifts-for-grandparents) ,[gifts for your wife](https://mitohealth.com/blog/gifts-for-wife) , and[gifts for your husband](https://mitohealth.com/blog/gifts-for-husband) .
